evidence.label: Finite generation for the K(n)-local sphere

headline: Claims every homotopy group of the K(n)-local sphere is finitely generated over the p-adic integers.
scope: Every prime p, every positive height n and every integer degree, and any finite p-local spectrum after K(n)-localization.
plain: The K(n)-local sphere isolates one chromatic layer of the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Its rational part was already known, but its torsion part could in principle be infinitely large in some degree. Hovey and Strickland asked whether each homotopy group is finitely generated over the p-adic integers. This paper claims yes, at every prime and height. It gives no uniform bound on the number of generators.
doesNot: This does not give a uniform bound on the number of generators or the torsion size across primes, heights or degrees.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mark Hovey and Neil Strickland, Morava K-theories and localisation, Problem 16.2
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers a standard finiteness question in chromatic homotopy theory at every height, where earlier proofs covered height one and height two for large primes.

explanation:
Start with a group that is small in one sense but large in another. Take infinitely many copies of the integers mod p, side by side. Every element gives zero when multiplied by p. Allowing fractions kills the whole group, so its rational part is zero. Yet no finite list of elements generates it[4]. So knowing the rational part says nothing about the size of the torsion.

The K(n)-local sphere is a piece of stable homotopy theory that isolates one chromatic height n. Its homotopy groups live in every integer degree, including negative ones[10]. Barthel, Schlank, Stapleton and Weinstein found the rational answer at every prime and height[3]. It is an exterior algebra on n generators in degrees −1, −3, −5 and so on. At height 2 this gives one rational copy in each of the degrees 0, −1, −3 and −4. At height 3 there are 8 such copies in total. But as the example shows, this leaves the torsion open.

Hovey and Strickland asked whether each homotopy group is finitely generated over the p-adic integers ℤ_p. Height one was known from a classical calculation. At height two and p at least 5, their analysis of Shimomura's calculations gave the answer[9]. The paper claims a yes at every prime, every positive height and every degree[1]. This answers their question[2]. In particular, the torsion part is finite in each degree[5].

The route goes through the Moore spectrum, the version of the sphere with p divided out. Known spectral sequence tools reduce the problem to a finiteness statement about group cohomology. Group cohomology measures how a group acts on a module. If that is finite for the Moore spectrum, the homotopy is finite in each degree[6]. Proving that finiteness is the main task of the paper[7]. It works down through the heights one at a time[11]. It uses the geometry of the Fargues–Fontaine curve, an object from p-adic geometry. No uniform bound on the number of generators is claimed[8].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The paper is long and draws on deep tools from p-adic geometry. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. It is a qualitative finiteness result with no uniform bound. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The part of the sphere's stable homotopy theory seen by the Morava K-theory at height n.
The index n of a layer in chromatic homotopy theory.
Every element can be built from a fixed finite list of elements.
A number system in which numbers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of p.
Elements that give zero when multiplied by some whole number.
The version of the sphere in which multiplication by p is divided out.

claims.sourceQuote: We prove that the homotopy groups of the $K(n)$-local sphere are finitely generated $\mathbb Z_p$-modules in every integer degree, for every prime $p$ and positive height $n$.
